script_body: The central market of Les Halles was Paris's pulsating lifeblood for nearly eight hundred years. In 1135, Louis VI set up a primitive market on land allotted by the Bishop of Paris, against a return of a third of its revenue. The marshy fields around it gave it its first name — Les Champeaux. In 1183, Philippe-Auguste replaced the open market with two stone buildings to shelter goods and vendors in bad weather, securing them with locks to prevent thefts. To raise the funds for the project, he confiscated the possessions of the Jews. The market became known as Les Halles — 'pour ce que chacun y allait,' for everyone went there — and the name stuck for eight centuries.

unverified_claims: Date 1135 vs 1137 — sources disagree. Book uses 1135, kept per editorial decision.

script_body: By the mid-19th century, France had entered the Industrial Age and iron was replacing stone. Impressed by Victor Baltard's newly built Gare de l'Est, Napoleon III commissioned him to rebuild the Les Halles market with a memorable instruction: 'Faites-moi des parapluies!' — make me umbrellas. Fourteen iron pavilions rose between 1851 and 1857, an artistic expression of the Industrial Revolution that stood for over a century. In 1969, the market was controversially transferred to Rungis south of Paris and the pavilions demolished. Only one of the fourteen survived, moved to the suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne. Sculptor Raymond Mason mourned: 'It was a place of bliss... the last vision of natural life in the City. It is now Paradise lost.' Social observer Louis Chevalier was blunter: 'The death of Les Halles has tolled the knell of Paris.'

script_body: Emile Zola dubbed Les Halles 'the belly of Paris,' a metaphor he used in 1873 for the title of one of his novels. For a year he haunted the market at all hours, recording the ever-changing hues of this gigantic digestive apparatus of the capital: dark bluish-grey metal structures against a light grey sky in wet weather, sheets of gold as the sun's rays penetrate on a fine day, glowing glass panes at sunset. He watched the robust porters — les forts des Halles, 'all nerves and muscles' — and descended into the undisclosable underground depths where the slaughter of fowl was carried out nightly, a place reeking of blood and pestilence and overrun by rats. This underworld was unknown to the bourgeois and the artist who, after a night at a cabaret, would drift to the market for onion soup and strong emotions.

script_body: The Dames des Halles — the market's notorious fishwives — occupied a unique position in Parisian society. On special occasions they were allowed into the King's Palace to pay their respects to the royal couple, and after a hearty meal they would return to Les Halles to pass on the latest Palace gossip. On 30 August 1608, one Femme Ladoucette wrote an astonishing letter to Marie de Medici, Henri IV's second wife. Having introduced herself as Dame des Halles 'from mother to daughter since Saint Louis,' she proceeded to complain about the King's philandering: a good fellow deep down, she wrote, but who 'fidgets at the sight of a coquette and scatters bastards around, although blessed with a most appetising Queen, so well conditioned to have little princes.' If the King wandered through Les Halles, she threatened, she would give him a sound thrashing for the love of her Queen. Femme Ladoucette received no scolding — instead she was promoted 'fournisseuse royale.'

script_body: With its ceaseless human tide, Les Halles was picked out for public executions and punishments from the 14th century onward. Decapitations were preceded by customary torture and followed by the mutilation of bodies. The King's pillory, the largest of them all, was a sizeable octagonal structure with a pointed roof and weathervane, somewhat resembling a chapel. The ground floor was often inhabited by the King's Great Executioner, while the convicts were exposed in the tower above. The excited mob relished the spectacle, taunting exposed victims and pelting them with rubbish and litter. There were no gallows, however — the King conceding that the market was no place for bodies to be left rotting on a rope.

script_body: The Ile de la Cite was the first part of Paris to be settled, occupied by the Celtic tribe of the Parisii in the 3rd century BC, making it the original nucleus of the city. In the 4th century AD, the Roman Emperor Julian established his seat on the island, on the site of today's Palais de Justice — it was here in 360 that he was proclaimed emperor by his own soldiers. In the 6th century, the Merovingian king Childebert made it the permanent home of the kings of France. And in the 13th century, the pious Louis IX built a private chapel adjoining the palace — la Chapelle Royale, now known as la Sainte-Chapelle — to house a piece of the Holy Cross and the Crown of Thorns he had bought from the last Emperor of Constantinople.

script_body: French haute couture was born not on the grand boulevards of the 8th arrondissement where it lives today, but right here in the 1st — in the second half of the 19th century. The world of fashion concentrated around Place Vendome and the Tuileries to serve Empress Eugenie and the ladies of the Napoleonic nobility. Its illustrious forerunner was Charles Worth, the Empress's English couturier — a fitting irony that the most French of industries was pioneered by an Englishman. The legendary Ritz hotel opened on Place Vendome catering predominantly to affluent English visitors, who also frequented the fabulous jewellery shops on rue de Castiglione and rue de la Paix. For their convenience, WH Smith opened a Parisian branch at no. 248 rue de Rivoli. It would take another century for haute couture's centre of gravity to shift westward to the 8th arrondissement.

script_body: In the 13th century, rue de la Ferronnerie — just steps from Les Halles — was the stronghold of the iron trade after which it was named: a narrow, congested street cluttered with blacksmiths' and ironmongers' stalls. It was still much the same on 14 May 1610 when the royal coach carrying Henri IV was held up in traffic on his way from the Louvre to the Arsenal near the Bastille, where his minister Sully was residing. The King was absorbed in a letter when a man named Ravaillac jumped onto the coach and stabbed him to death. Ravaillac was declared mentally deranged but was nevertheless sentenced to be drawn and quartered on Place de Grève — today's Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville — a sentence speedily carried out just thirteen days after the crime.

script_body: At no. 93 rue Saint-Honoré, an apothecary bore witness to two of France's most traumatic royal events across nearly two centuries. An apothecary was already trading here on 14 May 1610, when Henri IV was stabbed by Ravaillac on the neighbouring rue de la Ferronnerie. One hundred and eighty-three years later, on the day of Marie-Antoinette's execution on 16 October 1793, the successor apothecary at the same address closed his shop 'Au Bourdon d'Or' as a sign of mourning.

script_body: Henri IV's early amorous adventures had gained him the affectionate nickname 'le Vert Galant' — the amorous youth. But the charm faded as he grew older. The population resented the fact that he had at least eleven illegitimate children scattered throughout the kingdom, which all but plunged France into civil strife yet again. Furthermore, he had expressed his intention to marry his favourite mistress, Gabrielle d'Estrées — an outrage to the raison d'état. Only her premature death prevented this infamy. As Femme Ladoucette, a Dame des Halles, had expressed it in her letter to the Queen: in the kingdom of France, one separated the sheep from the goats. The assassination on rue de la Ferronnerie in 1610 was not the first attempt on the King's life — his scandalous personal conduct had made him many enemies.

script_body: The corner house at 2 rue Sauval, in the heart of Les Halles, was the birthplace of Molière in 1622 — the playwright whose stormy funeral at Saint-Eustache nearby would one day require the King's personal intervention. The original house was later demolished and replaced by the one still standing today, where the composer Richard Wagner reportedly stayed in 1839.

Nearby, at no. 6 rue Coquillère, Le Pied de Cochon has preserved its Belle Époque setting and still serves its famous onion soup.

script_body: In 1298, the extravagant Philippe le Bel ordered the reconstruction of a new palace on the Île de la Cité — 'the most beautiful that anyone in France ever saw.' Its Great Hall has survived as today's Salle des Pas Perdus. In its medieval heyday, the hall consisted of two naves separated by eight pillars, with a black-and-white chequered floor and polychrome walls. A huge marble table served both for sumptuous Gargantuan meals and as a stage for mystery plays, farces and other entertainments. Horrific skins of ferocious animals hung from the vaulted ceilings, and nobody seemed to mind the barbaric goings-on literally next door in the Conciergerie prison. The statues of every king of France stood against the pillars, gloriously painted in azure and gold — 58 in all by 1618, when a fire burnt down the hall with all its contents. Henri III had used the last available space for his own statue.

script_body: With King Jean II le Bon held captive in England, the provost of merchants Étienne Marcel reckoned on English support and believed he could overthrow the monarchy. On 22 February 1358, the Dauphin — the future Charles V — was sitting with two of his counsellors in the palace on the Île de la Cité when Marcel's men erupted in and slew the counsellors before his very eyes. The gushing blood of the victims stained the Dauphin's clothes, an experience he was never going to forget. A prudent politician, deservedly known as 'le Sage,' he left the palace one night stealthily by way of the river and moved to the Hôtel de Saint-Pol in the Marais, then arranged a residence within the safer walls of the Louvre, where he spent time from 1368 on. The kings of France never returned to the island, and the premises were taken over by the parliament — then the kingdom's court of justice.

script_body: At no. 1 quai de l'Horloge stands the entrance to the Conciergerie — originally the seat of the governor of the King's palace, hence its name. It became a prison in 1391 and remained so until 1934. Not unlike a modern concierge supplementing his income, the Palace concierge profited from vendors who leased the many shops within the Palace walls. But the prison's reality was far darker. In the 15th century, passers-by could still hear the screams of tortured prisoners in the Tour Bonbec — the most westerly tower. The name 'bon-bec' (meaning 'prate' in the Middle Ages) probably alluded to the interrogations on the ground floor: a varied spectrum of torture methods was devised to make victims confess and denounce their accomplices. During a restoration in 1828, two oubliettes were found in the tower's basement, communicating with the river and spiked with iron points — needless to dwell on the fate of the prisoners.

script_body: Among the notorious prisoners of the Conciergerie were Ravaillac, the assassin of Henri IV; the mass poisoner La Marquise de Brinvilliers (1630-1676), who had eliminated the better part of her numerous household; and Cartouche (1693-1721), the most notorious bandit of his age and the terror of Paris. To be admitted into Cartouche's prestigious gang, a candidate had to prove himself an expert cutpurse. Candidates were made to practise on dummies covered with little bells until they could strip them clean without the slightest tinkling. All three prisoners awaited execution at the Conciergerie.

script_body: During the Revolution, the Conciergerie boasted an impressive list of illustrious prisoners awaiting their deaths. Madame Roland, who had supported the Revolution but sided with the Girondins at the wrong time. Marie-Antoinette, who occupied a dreary cell from 2 August to 16 October 1793, when she was taken to the guillotine on Place de la Révolution. Then Danton, Robespierre and Saint-Just were detained here in their turn — Danton and Robespierre occupying the cells adjacent to the Queen's. In all, some 2,780 victims of the Revolutionary Tribunal passed through the arcade entrance to the jeers of delighted tricoteuses huddled on the perron.

script_body: North of the Conciergerie's Gothic halls was a section of the prison leading to the dark cells, known as 'rue de Paris' — named after the Great Executioner, Monsieur de Paris. This post was held by seven successive generations of the Sanson family, from 1688 to 1847, transmitted from father to son. Shortly before the Revolution, Louis XVI had set his heart on improving their plight and granted Charles-Henri Sanson an annual fee of 16,000 pounds plus 2,000 crowns for the upkeep of the scaffold and pillory — never suspecting he would become his own executioner. Being a royalist, Charles-Henri had no desire to carry out that deed. On 15 August 1792 he was arrested as 'the despot's employee'; with each execution he would be dispatched from his cell to Place du Carrousel, where the guillotine stood, and afterwards taken back. When the guillotine began to work at full swing and his expert hand could not be dispensed with, he was released — but retired soon after executing his sovereign. His son Henri held the position during the Terror and beyond, until 1840. The film-maker Jean Renoir marvelled that his own grandfather — the painter's father, a tailor from Limoges — had known Henri's chief assistant during the Terror: a man who 'may have passed Voltaire and Benjamin Franklin in the street, heard Mozart play the harpsichord.' Old Renoir befriended the assistant, and as Jean Renoir observed: 'After all, they were two good workmen: one cut out cloth, the other cut off heads just as conscientiously.'

script_body: Place Vendôme sums up the switchback history of 19th-century France in a single column. Girardon's original equestrian statue of the Sun King was disposed of during the Revolution. Napoleon's Colonne d'Austerlitz replaced it in 1810. With the Restoration, it was swapped for an equestrian Henri IV, le Vert Galant. When the bourgeois Louis-Philippe took the throne, the Vert Galant was dispatched to the Pont-Neuf and a Napoleon in a frock coat was set up instead — which his nephew Napoleon III later substituted with an imperial Napoleon as a Roman Caesar. In 1871 the Commune, led by the painter Courbet, toppled the column to the sound of the Marseillaise as thousands of patriots cheered. The Emperor regained his lofty position the following year when the bourgeois National Assembly sent him back to the top. He has been dominating this mecca of luxury ever since.

script_body: In 451, Attila the Hun was at the gates of Paris with his army. The terrified population was ready to flee the left bank, but Genevieve bolstered their courage, prophesying that Paris would be spared. Though romanticized as a shepherdess in the 17th century, Genevieve was born in Nanterre to a well-to-do Roman father and a Greek mother. She led an ascetic life devoted to the poor and sick, performed miracles, and her prophecy came true. She became the patron saint of Paris. It was under her guidance — and through the influence of his wife Clotilde — that King Clovis converted to Christianity and made Paris his capital. The basilica of Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul was built on this hilltop site, receiving in its crypt both Clovis, who died in 511, and Genevieve, who died in 512 aged 89.
key_claims: Clovis converted under Genevieve and Clotilde

script_body: Genevieve's reliquary, fashioned around 630 by the famous Saint Eloi — patron of goldsmiths and later minister to King Dagobert I — was chiselled in gold and studded with gems. In times of floods, epidemics, and calamities, following a day of penitence and fasting, it would be carried in procession to Notre-Dame through streets decked with multicoloured drapery and strewn with flowers, to the continuous chiming of all the city's church bells. The story goes that during a raging epidemic in 1130, all were cured except three sceptics who would not prostrate themselves and therefore died. By 1725 there had been 114 such processions. In November 1793, the Revolution stripped the reliquary of its precious stones and sent it to the Mint. Genevieve's remains were burnt on Place de Greve.
source_passage: Genevieve's reliquary was fashioned in 630 by the famous Saint Eloi

script_body: In November 1793, the Revolution's anti-clerical fervour reached Saint Genevieve. Her reliquary was stripped of its precious stones and sent to the Mint to be melted down. Against all logic, the remains of Saint Genevieve — who had embodied precisely the same ideals as the Revolution, feeding the poor and defending Paris — were burnt on Place de Greve. In one fell swoop, the Revolution destroyed twelve hundred years of devotion. The wooden sculptures of the reliquary survived, though they lost their arms, and are now in the Louvre. In 1803, a fragment of the saint's sarcophagus was discovered in the crypt and placed in a new reliquary above the altar of Saint-Etienne-du-Mont, where it remains today.
source_passage: In November 1793 the reliquary was stripped of its precious stones and sent to the Mint to be melted down

script_body: The Revolution swept away the great Abbey of Sainte-Genevieve, founded in the 7th century by monks who settled next to Genevieve's holy shrine. But vestiges survive, now part of the Lycee Henri IV: medieval vaults, kitchens, a refectory, a cloister, the grand staircase dating from the 18th century, and the dome of the abbey's magnificent library. The square church tower on rue Clovis is the only element remaining in its original position. The abbey was a great place of learning, closely bound with the medieval University — its abbot held the post of chancellor and presented diplomas to graduates.

script_body: In 1640, Louis XIII chose a pleasant area on the sunny side of the 5th arrondissement as the site for a royal botanic garden for medicinal herbs, as suggested by his physician Jean Herouard. The Jardin Royal des Plantes Medicinales gathered 1,800 different plants for medical students. For two centuries, scientists of world renown developed natural science here: Cuvier, the father of paleontology; Buffon, who devoted decades to his Histoire Naturelle; and many others — Thouin, Tournefort, Linne, Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, the Jussieu family — all now honoured in the surrounding street names.

The imposing arena was the second largest in all of Gaul after that of Nimes. It faced east to take advantage of the natural east-facing slope and the setting sun, which lit up the podium, with the pastoral Bievre meandering through green meadows towards the Seine in the background.

The church was built in the late 15th century when the adjacent abbey church grew too small. Its interior is striking for its asymmetrical structure, the ornate 17th-century organ, and fabulous 16th- and 17th-century stained glass displayed in the cloister of the Chapelle des Catechismes.

script_body: Here lie the remains of Pascal and Racine, but more importantly, the relics of Saint Genevieve herself. They rest in a brass reliquary — a poor 19th-century substitute for the bejewelled original that vanished in the fury of the Revolution in 1793. The stone underneath was rescued from the abbey's crypt and is believed to be part of the Saint's original sarcophagus. On 6 September 1914, with Germans at the gates of Paris, Parisians thronged here to pray, just as they had faced the Huns 1500 years before. When the war ended, many returned to leave plaques of gratitude on the chapel walls.

script_body: Across rue Clovis, the Tour Clovis is the only remnant of the old abbey church of Sainte-Genevieve, which was abandoned, its Gothic style having gone out of fashion, torn down in 1790, and replaced by rue Clovis. The tower lost its spire in 1750 and is now enclosed within the prestigious Lycee Henri IV, founded after the Revolution. Its pupils included Alfred de Musset, Viollet-le-Duc, Baron Haussmann, and all the sons of Louis-Philippe. French schools being sealed to outsiders, you can only peep through the doorway to glimpse the lovely flower-filled courtyard and the abbey library, now the school dining room.

script_body: Next to the main entrance on rue Buffon stands the spacious 18th-century hotel bought by Buffon in 1772 to serve as the director's residence. Thomas Jefferson was a dinner guest here several times and both admired Buffon — 'a man of extraordinary powers in conversation' — and was warily deferential. Buffon died here fulfilled and happy in 1788, at age 80, just in time to avoid the Revolution. Under his supervision and with Louis XVI's support, the gardens reached their peak, containing some 10,000 species of plants, a tropical glasshouse, the trunk of a 2,000-year-old sequoia, and a cedar of Lebanon brought by Jussieu in 1734.

script_body: On 9 July 1827, Charles X was offered a giraffe as a present from the Pasha of Egypt — the first giraffe to tread French soil. Named Zarafa, she was paraded through the streets on her way to the Jardin des Plantes, cheered by enthusiastic crowds. Over 600,000 Parisians jostled to see her. Paris was gripped by a giraffe craze — images appeared on brooches, combs, umbrellas, anything one could find. But in the terrible winter of 1870-71, when Prussians besieged Paris, starving citizens invaded the menagerie and devoured all its animals, along with the rats and cats of the capital.

script_body: Nobody believed the Roman arena really existed until the 1860s, when workmen building rue Monge stumbled upon it accidentally. Haussmann's remodelling was not to be hindered by such trifles: in 1870, two-thirds of the unearthed arena were demolished for new apartment blocks and an omnibus depot. The last third, dug up in 1883, was likewise marked for destruction, but Victor Hugo intervened. 'It is not possible,' he wrote, 'that Paris, the city of the future, should renounce the living proof that it was a city of the past.' What you see today is the original surviving section plus a 1918 reconstruction of the demolished portion.

script_body: The abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Pres began as a basilica in the late 6th century. A deed from December 6, 558 records Childebert, son of Clovis, declaring 'I have begun to build a church.' The Bishop of Paris, Saint Germain, urged Childebert to erect a sanctuary for Saint Vincent, the patron of wine-growers. A relic of Saint Vincent's tunic and a gold cross said to have belonged to King Solomon were laid in the new basilica. Saint Germain had it decorated with magnificent mosaics and topped with a gilded roof, glittering amidst peaceful meadows — earning it the nickname Saint-Germain-le-Dore. The church tower that still dominates the Place pierced the skies of Paris less than a century later, and on 21 April 1163, the completed church was consecrated by Pope Alexander III.

script_body: Three centuries after his death, Saint Germain reportedly defended his abbey against the Norsemen through supernatural intervention, as recorded by a monk named Abbon. One Danish brigand was tied to a chariot by the invisible Saint, then chased into hell by Death. Another lost his way on a turret and rolled off the steep roof. A third lost his sight when he turned his eyes toward the Saint's sepulchre, while a fourth was snatched away from above by the Saint's invisible hand. Abbon's testimony increased the prestige of Saint Germain as the patriot who fought back the invincible Dane.
source_passage: it was thanks to Saint Germain's supernatural intervention that the abbey set up a heroic resistance to the Norsemen

script_body: When Paris was liberated, the entire neighbourhood of Saint-Germain blazed into freedom. Boris Vian and his friends celebrated with trumpet blasts through the small hours at the Tabou on rue Dauphine. Claude Luter brought his unbridled clarinet and Dixieland to the basement of Lorientais. Club Saint-Germain at 13 rue Saint-Benoit picked up the baton in 1948, hosting Charlie Parker, Coleman Hawkins, Duke Ellington and Miles Davis. Meanwhile, Juliette Greco, dressed in all-purpose black, became the spokeswoman of existentialist Saint-Germain, singing to lyrics by Sartre, Queneau and Prevert. A new generation of anti-establishment singer-poets — Georges Brassens, Jacques Brel, Leo Ferre — made their appearance in vaulted cabarets.

script_body: American expatriates flooded Saint-Germain in the 1920s, making good use of the favourable dollar exchange rate and breaking loose from Prohibition. The newly-wed Hemingways, arriving in December 1921, could enjoy a hearty meal at the Pre-aux-Clercs on the corner of rue Jacob and rue Bonaparte for just 6 francs. Natalie Barney's literary salon at 20 rue Jacob, with its charming ivy-overgrown courtyard, gathered the beautiful people in a mock Greek temple dubbed Le Temple de l'Amitie. Gertrude Stein opened her home at 27 rue de Fleurus to chosen writers, while Sylvia Beach published and sold their works through Shakespeare and Company at 12 rue de l'Odeon — including James Joyce's Ulysses in 1922.

script_body: Rue Dauphine commemorates the Dauphin and future Louis XIII and was opened by Henri IV as a continuation of the Pont-Neuf and Place Dauphine. The Augustine monks protested the new street would encroach on their grounds, but Henri IV was a man of vision and refused to bend, saying he would use his guns to carry his project through if he had to. He argued the monks would draw greater income from houses along the new street than from their cabbage-beds. History proved him right: on the eve of the Revolution, their order was one of the wealthiest in the capital. Rue Dauphine became one of the most elegant arteries, especially after 1763 when it was the first to substitute oil lamps for candles.

Look carefully at the second chancel — those small columns are survivors from the original 6th-century basilica that honoured Saint Vincent, before Saint Germain took over as patron. In 1163, a larger choir was built to accommodate growing numbers of monks, along with a bell-tower and majestic portal. Pope Alexander III himself presided over the ceremony — and just weeks later, he would lay the cornerstone of Notre-Dame cathedral across the river.

script_body: On 2 September 1792, the abbey prison that once stood across Boulevard Saint-Germain became the site of one of the Revolution's bloodiest episodes. Rumours of a plot against 'the good people' of Paris were deliberately spread, bells were rung, pamphlets distributed. After a mock trial, 100 prisoners including many priests were executed on the first day. By the third day, hundreds had been killed at or near the junction of rue Bonaparte and rue de l'Abbaye, their bodies piled in the abbey gardens. The killers worked by torchlight through the night, then tried to erase all evidence, ordering prison concierges to wash away blood with water and vinegar.

script_body: The abbey of Saint-Germain was once a city within a city, home to about 10,000 people, its domains reaching into today's 15th arrondissement. It answered directly to the Pope, ensuring political independence. Its 13th-century chapel, designed by Pierre de Montreuil — the same architect behind Sainte-Chapelle — was destroyed during the Revolution. When 15,000 tons of gunpowder stored in the dining hall ignited alongside a huge stock of coal, the explosion and fire devoured nearly everything, including a library of 50,000 volumes. Yet miraculously, most of its 7,000 manuscripts survived, including Pascal's original Pensées.

Victor Baltard undertook its restoration, while Hippolyte Flandrin contributed the murals you can see inside.

script_body: The Eiffel Tower was designed not by Eiffel himself but by two engineers in his company, Koechlin and Nouguier, whose project won the competition for a striking monument for the 1889 Universal Exhibition. The Exhibition officially commemorated the centenary of the French Revolution — among competing proposals was a gigantic guillotine in honour of the victims of the Terror. Rising approximately 312 metres, the Tower was twice the height of the tallest structure previously built by man. Despite its gigantic dimensions, the iron structure weighed roughly 7,300 tonnes — an awesome technical feat. Yet on 7 May 1889, the day of its solemn inauguration, none of the lifts worked.

script_body: Not everyone welcomed the Tower. A petition signed by fifty leading figures from arts and letters — including Guy de Maupassant, Charles Gounod, Alexandre Dumas, and Charles Garnier — condemned the 'monstrous construction' in the name of Art and Civilisation. They showered it with metaphors: 'hollow candlestick', 'solitary riddled suppository', 'bald umbrella', 'skeleton'. Maupassant, contemplating leaving Paris, settled instead for lunching in the second-floor restaurant — the only spot in the city from which the Tower could not be seen. The painter Robert Delaunay saw it differently, making the Tower his favourite subject.

script_body: The Tower was meant to be ephemeral — a temporary structure for the World's Fair — and in 1909 enemies intensified campaigns to demolish it, claiming it was useless. Its salvation came from its height: wireless telegraphy was emerging, and the tall iron tower made a marvellous antenna. The first spoken news bulletin was broadcast from the Eiffel Tower in 1925, and in 1935 France's first experimental television transmission was made from here — a milestone that a few dozen excited enthusiasts received on their sets.

script_body: On 31 March 1889, the second anniversary of the beginning of construction, a sixty-strong party of top-hatted and monocled dignitaries made the first official ascent. Prime Minister Gustave Tirard gave up at the first floor; most of the others followed. But Gustave Eiffel persevered, urging the last ten breathless participants to the summit, where — with Paris spread at his feet — the Minister of Trade awarded him the Légion d'honneur. The honour, the book notes, should rightly have been shared with the two original designers, Koechlin and Nouguier.

script_body: The 1889 Universal Exhibition, and the Eiffel Tower at its heart, was not merely a celebration of engineering. The Third Republic, beleaguered by anarchists, revisionists and Boulangistes threatening its stability, organised the Exhibition to boost patriotic feeling and achieve political cohesion. It was to mark the Republic's recovery and trumpet France's entry into modernity — to dazzle the world and assert national prestige at a moment of profound internal vulnerability.

script_body: How ironic to recall that 300 prominent members of the intelligentsia signed a petition against the Eiffel Tower's erection, calling it a crime against history and against Paris. Yet it survived its planned demolition and became the unassailable emblem of the city. Even visitors familiar with skyscrapers feel overwhelmed as they approach it: 18,038 metal pieces held together by 2.5 million rivets weighing 7,300 tonnes — an extraordinary technological feat.

script_body: The Tower has attracted both the heroic and the desperate. Eccentrics attempted to fly from it with homemade wings — an Austrian called Reichelt in 1912 hit the ground head first. In 1977 a French stunt man flew a hang-glider from the first floor; an English couple parachuted from the third; an American pilot flew between its legs and lost his licence. Of the 380 people who have hurled themselves from the Tower, only one escaped death — a young woman in 1964 who landed on the roof of a parked car. That year suicides averaged one per month, after which parapets were installed.

script_body: During World War I, the Eiffel Tower played a crucial military role: Mata Hari, the infamous dancer-spy, was identified through radio transmissions intercepted at the Tower's wireless station. Coded messages sent by a German contact referred to agent 'H21' — swiftly identified as Mata Hari. She was captured and shot on 15 October 1917. Nearly 50,000 words were received and transmitted from the Tower during that war — alone a compelling reason not to demolish it.

script_body: Marie Curie lived at 36 quai de Bethune from 1912 to 1934. Nearby, the cosmetics magnate Helena Rubinstein purchased a Le Vau mansion in 1932 — and to the horror of preservationists, demolished it in 1935 to build a modernist replacement.

Place de Greve hosted the fete de la Saint-Jean on 24 June, when a 10-metre-high bonfire celebrated the birth of John the Baptist. Occasionally the King himself would come to light the fire, heralded by trumpets.

Place Royale was a favourite site for duels, watched from balconies by ladies whose favours were being sought. Cardinal Richelieu banned duels in 1626. When Boutteville contravened the ruling, believing his glorious pedigree put him above the law, Richelieu had him decapitated at Place de Greve.

Parisians, never short of a cutting nickname, dubbed the Centre Pompidou 'Notre-Dame-des-Tuyaux' — Our Lady of the Pipes. The irreverent name captures both the outrage and the grudging affection Parisians developed for the building's industrial aesthetic in the heart of their historic city.

At 36 rue des Tournelles, just steps from this square, the legendary Ninon Lenclos held court in a modest house where Molière, Boileau, La Fontaine and the Duc d'Orléans brought their own food in recognition of their hosts' slender means. Ninon transformed what in others was scandalous prostitution into a socially acceptable way of life — 'the triumph of vice conducted with wit,' as Saint-Simon put it. She was irresistible to the greatest men of France, welcoming them all into her generous bed. The puritanical Anne of Austria eventually had her locked up in the Madelonnettes, a convent-prison for repentant prostitutes — despite Ninon's famous protest that she was 'neither a whore nor repentant.' Undaunted, she ate ostentatiously during Lent and threw her meat bone out the window — a brave act when impiety was punishable by death.

Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano designed the Centre Georges Pompidou with bright blue building and bright red and blue piping. Parisians were scandalized that two 'hippy' architects built a 'refinery' in the historic heart of Paris — twenty years later it still ranked first among monuments they wished to see wiped out. Yet it drew 28,000 visitors per day and 8 million per year, beating the Eiffel Tower's 2.5 million.

The anti-bourgeois proletarian Commune burnt down the Hotel de Ville in 1871. The victorious bourgeois government of the Third Republic rebuilt it at once in its old style, to brush off this incident and demonstrate that its possession was irrevocable.

Notre-Dame endured centuries of vandalism before the Revolution even began. The medieval chancel screen was destroyed in 1699 to make way for a more fashionable baroque interior. The original stained glass windows — except for the three great rose windows — were ripped out and replaced with plain white glass to 'let in more light.'

Eugene Viollet-le-Duc began his controversial restoration of Notre-Dame in 1844, guided by his famous principle: 'To restore a building is not to maintain it, repair it, or rebuild it; it is to re-establish it in a complete state which may never have existed at any given moment.' He added the spire, the gargoyles, and much of what the world came to think of as 'original' medieval decoration.

The Marais in its golden age was studded with magnificent hotels. Great architects Mansart and Le Vau and painters Le Brun, Mignard and Vouet decorated the interiors. The Duc de Richelieu sold ten Nicolas Poussin paintings to Louis XIV and bought some twenty Rubens to replace them.

The municipality of Paris grew from the corporation of water merchants who bought the strand (greve) from Louis VII in the 12th century. A tribunal of commerce was set up on Place de Greve, becoming the embryo of the municipality. The corporation's seal, inherited from the ancient Nautae Parisiaci, remains the coat of arms of Paris with only minor changes a thousand years later.

The Pavillon du Roi dominates the south side of the square, grander than the other 36 houses that form the harmonious ensemble. The square was inaugurated in 1612 with a spectacular three-day celebration for the double wedding of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, and his sister Elisabeth with the future Philip IV of Spain. It was renamed Place des Vosges in 1800, honouring the first department to pay its taxes to the new Republic.
With the court's transfer to Versailles in 1682, the Marais declined. In 1962, Andre Malraux's rehabilitation bill passed; in 1965 the area was declared a protected zone.

Henri IV dreamed of making Paris a centre of silk manufacture, hoping to rival Lyon and undercut costly Italian imports. He brought 200 Italian workers to the site of this square and planted mulberry trees for their silkworms. But the northern climate defeated the enterprise — the silkworms simply could not survive Parisian winters, and the project was abandoned.

Place Royale (now Place des Vosges) was the first open-air square in Paris. Its exquisite bright pink brick and white stone pavilions served in 1612 as the backdrop for the most dazzling celebration recalled by Parisians: the double wedding of Louis XIII and his sister Elisabeth.

The quai des Balcons earned its name from the series of ornate iron balconies lining its facades. The 18th-century writer Mercier observed that the island had 'its own moral code, its own customs' — a village within Paris that to this day retains an insular, self-contained atmosphere quite unlike the rest of the city.

In Rabelais's tale, the giant Gargantua visited Notre-Dame and, followed and gawked at by Parisians, climbed the church tower and urinated on the crowd below, drowning 260,418 people (exclusive of women and children). In Rabelais's version, the city of Lutetia became known as Paris — from 'par rie' (for a laugh) — in recognition of Gargantua's jest.

Victor Hugo's 1831 novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame was written partly as a plea to save the crumbling cathedral. The book ignited a wave of public passion for the medieval monument and directly led to the campaign for its restoration — proof that a novel can save a building.

Look up. Every rivet you see was placed by hand — 2.5 million of them. Gustave Eiffel didn't build this for beauty; he built it to prove iron could touch the sky. Parisians called it an eyesore. Now it's the most visited paid monument on Earth.

Notre-Dame hosted only two coronations, both controversial: Henry VI of England, who had conquered France, and Emperor Napoleon. The legitimate French dynasties always used the cathedral of Reims. Henri IV's conversion to Catholicism was celebrated here in 1593 with a Te Deum, though the conversion ceremony itself took place at Saint-Denis.

The Bastille was far from the grim dungeon of popular imagination. It functioned as a luxury prison for well-connected inmates. Voltaire completed his tragedy Oedipe here, composing verses and dining well. The Marquis de Sade draped his cell walls with fabric and had his own furniture brought in. When the fortress was finally stormed on July 14, 1789, the liberators found only seven prisoners inside — a far cry from the hundreds the revolutionaries imagined they would free.

The Centre Pompidou's piazza became a focal point of Parisian street life, with buskers, acrobats, mime artists, jugglers, fire-eaters, portrait painters and pickpockets spontaneously recreating the medieval atmosphere of the parvis of Notre-Dame.

Henri IV's plan for the first open-air square in Paris was carried through to completion after his death. Inaugurated to celebrate the double betrothal of Louis XIII to Anne of Austria and of his sister Elizabeth to the future Philip IV of Spain, the festivities began on 5 April 1612 and lasted three days: an extraordinary carousel of trumpets, oboes and violins paraded round the square, while the guns of the Bastille roared in the distance. At night, a torchlight procession wound through the streets of Paris and fireworks blazed over the Bastille. These events elevated the Marais to the undisputed aristocratic centre of 17th-century Paris.

Notre-Dame was the birthplace of polyphonic music in Europe. In the 12th and 13th centuries, the composers Leonin and Perotin developed the art of organum — music in multiple voices — at the cathedral's choir school. Their innovations laid the foundations for all Western harmony.

The Centre Pompidou was conceived as a transparent cultural centre for the people — a place where the inner workings of the building would be visible from the outside. The architects turned architecture inside out, placing all the structural elements, ducts, and escalators on the exterior, leaving the interior as open, flexible exhibition space.

Beneath Notre-Dame's chancel, vestiges of a pillar-shaped monument dedicated to Jupiter were found in 1711 — the Pilier des Nautes, erected by the corporation of water merchants (Nautae Parisiaci). Inscriptions date it to the reign of Emperor Tiberius (AD 14-37), making it the oldest sculpted monument found in the capital. The merchants engraved their own gods alongside those of Rome. The pillar is now displayed in the Musee National du Moyen Age at the Hotel de Cluny.

The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789 became the founding myth of the French Revolution, yet the reality was far less dramatic. Finance minister Necker had already drawn up plans to demolish the fortress. When the mob broke in, they found only seven bewildered prisoners — four forgers, two madmen, and a young nobleman imprisoned at his family's request.

On September 8, 1656, Christina of Sweden made a spectacular entry into the square. The former queen, who had abdicated her throne two years earlier, arrived in Paris amid great fanfare and was received with elaborate ceremony at Place Royale.

The restaurant Nos Ancetres les Gaulois on the island offers a distinctive dining experience — a ribald celebration of Gallic excess with unlimited wine and rustic fare, echoing the spirit of the Gauls who once inhabited this stretch of the Seine.

The Hotel de Bretonvilliers, once the most splendid mansion on the island, was destroyed — a casualty of the same forces of modernisation and neglect that threatened the entire Marais before its 20th-century rehabilitation.

Notre-Dame's great bell, known today as Emmanuel, has a dramatic history. The original bell, called Jacqueline, was recast in 1680 and renamed Emmanuel. According to tradition, the ladies of the court threw their jewellery into the molten metal, which is said to give the bell its exceptionally pure tone.

Philippe-Auguste confiscated the Jews' possessions and expelled them from the royal demesne in 1182. Their centuries-old presence on rue de la Juiverie, the central axis of the Ile de la Cite, came to an end. When he invited the Jews back 16 years later to squeeze them dry once more, they settled on the right bank around rue des Rosiers.

corrections.correction: In 1182 Philippe-Auguste did confiscate Jewish property (the beat's core is true), but two elements of the compound claim are inaccurate. (1) SCOPE: the 1182 edict expelled Jews from the royal demesne — the crown's directly-held lands, essentially the Île-de-France — not "France" as a whole. In 1182 the Kingdom of France was a patchwork of largely autonomous fiefs (Plantagenet Normandy/Anjou/Aquitaine, Champagne, Flanders, Burgundy, Toulouse), where Jews continued to live outside royal control.

script_body: Etienne Marcel, provost of Paris, was the first to settle the city government in a town hall on Place de Greve, buying a two-storeyed house from the king on behalf of the city in 1357. Known as La Maison des Piliers for its row of arcades, it was eventually replaced by a magnificent Renaissance building begun under Francois I.

The Ile Saint-Louis was developed in the first half of the 17th century, transforming two muddy islands — l'Ile Notre-Dame and l'Ile aux Vaches — into the elegant residential quarter you see today. Corneille marvelled at how 'a whole city had sprung from an old ditch.'

The Marquis de Sade was transferred to the Bastille from Vincennes in 1784. He fashioned a megaphone from a funnel and shouted to passersby that prisoners were being murdered inside. The authorities removed him in early July 1789 — just days before the storming. At the Bastille he wrote some of his most notorious works, including Justine.

After the Commune burned the original Hotel de Ville in 1871, the Third Republic rebuilt it with lavish interiors designed to project the permanence and grandeur of the new regime. Inside you'll find a bust by Rodin and magnificent murals by Puvis de Chavannes — some of the finest civic decorations in Paris.

Place de Greve was where people gathered in early morning to seek work, a practice called 'faire la greve.' The expression survives in modern French but now means 'to go on strike' — the opposite of its original meaning of seeking employment.

On Friday 17 July 1676, Madame de Sevigne watched the Marquise de Brinvilliers carried to Place de Greve. The Marquise had poisoned her father (requiring ten attempts) and two brothers. Her lover Godin de Sainte-Croix had learned the art of poison from an Italian named Exili while imprisoned in the Bastille. Sevigne wrote: 'At last, it is all over, the Brinvilliers is in the air.'

During the Paris Commune in May 1871, Communards attempted to burn Notre-Dame by piling chairs and furniture against the doors and setting them alight. Doctors and staff from the neighbouring Hotel-Dieu rushed across and extinguished the flames, saving the cathedral from destruction.

The 28 statues of the Kings of Judah on the west facade were torn down by Revolutionaries who mistook them for the Kings of France. The heads were discovered in 1977 during construction work near the Opera and are now displayed at the Musee de Cluny.

Between 1163 and 1330, anonymous artisans carved Notre-Dame from stone, slipping imperceptibly from the Romanesque to the Gothic style yet sustaining architectural unity. Bishop Maurice de Sully initiated the project, commissioning a monument to transcend every other in the kingdom.

The presence of royalty in the Marais ended brutally on 30 June 1559, when Henri II was fatally wounded during a friendly tournament in the gardens of the Hôtel des Tournelles — the site on which this square now stands. His opponent, the Comte de Montgomery, captain of the Scottish guard, shattered a lance that pierced the King's eye. Henri lingered for ten agonising days before dying on 10 July. His bereaved wife Catherine de Medici abandoned the accursed place at once, eventually settling at the newly built Palais des Tuileries. In 1565 she ordered the Hôtel des Tournelles razed to the ground, to blot it from her memory — inadvertently clearing the ground for Henri IV's masterpiece.

During the Revolution, Notre-Dame was nearly lost forever. Stripped of its treasures and rededicated to the Cult of Reason, it was put up for sale as building material. A certain Citoyen Simon nearly purchased the cathedral — one of the closest brushes with destruction in the building's history.

Place de Greve served as Paris's main place of public executions, with gallows as a permanent fixture. Notable executions included Cartouche, the terror of early 18th-century Paris; Ravaillac, assassin of Henri IV; and the Marquise de Brinvilliers, mass poisoner.

The Ile Saint-Louis was originally two separate islands: l'Ile Notre-Dame, serving as the cathedral's recreational grounds, and l'Ile aux Vaches, the domain of grazing cows, laundresses and lovers. During the 14th century, a defence tower with a moat divided them. In the first half of the 17th century, the moat was filled in and the two islands united into the Ile Saint-Louis.
